title: Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, in three recordings
work: Pomp and Circumstance — March No. 1, Op. 39
question: Elgar, Stock and the United States Marine Band play the march and the broadening of its trio tune.
intro: “I’ve got a tune that will knock ’em — knock ’em flat,” Elgar told Dora Penny in May 1901. Twenty-five years later he and Frederick Stock recorded the march on opposite sides of the Atlantic; Stock’s recording included Chicago’s grand organ. In the version by the United States Marine Band, wind and brass play the lines that strings play in the orchestral score.

recordings.label: Edward Elgar, 1926
recordings.note: The composer conducted the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra at Queen’s Hall, in his first complete recording of the march.

recordings.label: Frederick Stock, 1926
recordings.note: Stock brings together the Chicago Symphony and the organist Walter P. Zimmerman, whose grand organ reinforces the orchestra.

recordings.label: United States Marine Band
recordings.note: Wind and brass carry the tune in this concert-band arrangement; the strings’ bow strokes become tongued notes.

passages.label: Return of the quick march
passages.note: The quick march returns in D major. The strings play short phrases and fast runs above the bass.

passages.label: March before the trio
passages.note: Accented phrases keep the orchestra in march time; the long trio melody has not yet entered.

passages.label: Final trio, Molto maestoso
passages.note: The trio tune returns in D major, marked Molto maestoso. High violins play above the full orchestra.

passages.label: Broadening of the trio tune
passages.note: The tune broadens towards its final held notes. After the cadence, a last passage of quick march music follows.
